content: format_candidates is unsafe for multiline content. Memory entries are free text and can contain '\n', which corrupts the `id | kind | importance | content` pipe-delimited format sent to the LLM. The LLM can then mis-attribute ids to contents and emit merge/contradiction/distill ops that target the wrong rows, which get applied to the DB. Replace newlines in m.content (and ideally also '|' collisions) before formatting, e.g. `m.content.replace('\n', " ").replace('\r', " ")`, or use a structured JSON/serde prompt instead of a plain-text pipe format.
existing_code:
fn format_candidates(items: &[MemItem]) -> String {
    items
        .iter()
        .map(|m| format!("{} | {} | {} | {}", m.id, m.kind, m.importance, m.content))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join("\n")
}

content: gather_candidates loads the entire memory table into RAM on every tick. store::load_all is unbounded, then the OR-filter (updated_at_ms>=threshold || access_count>=N) is applied in memory before the LIMIT. Over months of use this becomes O(total_memories) per 10-minute tick, both CPU and heap. Push the WHERE clause into SQL (with the OR predicate) and apply LIMIT server-side; only fall back to in-memory filtering when an explicit ORDER BY + sort is needed.

Scheduler has no shutdown/cancellation and can overlap with manual runs. The spawned loop runs forever with no cancellation token, so on app exit it is dropped mid-LLM-call or mid-transaction (the inner spawn_blocking may still complete in background, producing orphaned DB writes). Independently, while the scheduler is awaiting run_consolidation (LLM call is not under DB_WRITE_LOCK), a manual memory_consolidate_now click issues a parallel LLM call against the same candidate snapshot — only the DB write path is serialized, so you waste API quota and can produce duplicate / interleaved ops that race at id resolution. Add a CancellationToken (or watch channel) the loop selects on alongside the ticker, and an in-flight flag (or DB-level advisory) to suppress the manual run while a scheduled run is active.

Every failure path inside `embed_text` collapses to `None` via `.ok()?` with zero logging: tokenizer encode errors, `Tensor::from_array` allocation errors, `Mutex` poisoning, `session.run` ONNX errors, `try_extract_tensor` shape/type mismatches, and the manual `data.len() != seq * EMBED_DIM` check. In production this makes silent embedding degradation completely invisible — the memory subsystem will quietly fall back to keyword-only recall with no telemetry to explain why. At minimum, gate a `log::debug!`/`eprintln!` (consistent with the existing init-time `eprintln!` style) on each path so failures are diagnosable.

Mutex poisoning recovery silently continues after a prior panic. `e.into_inner()` returns the locked guard without clearing the poison flag, so if any prior task panicked mid-transaction (e.g. inside `apply_reflection`'s tx before `commit()`), subsequent operations proceed on potentially inconsistent DB state with no integrity check. Consider treating a poisoned `DB_WRITE_LOCK` as a hard error for write paths (return Err) and only allow recovery for read paths, or at minimum require an admin-initiated reset before resuming writes.

Check-then-act race violates the documented "same key 覆盖" invariant. `find_by_key_tag` followed by either `update_by_id` or `insert_item_with` runs outside any transaction; two concurrent `remember_fact` calls with the same key can both observe `Ok(None)` and both insert, producing duplicate rows whose `tags[0]` equals the same key. `insert_item_with`'s semantic dedup is by embedding cosine, not by `tags[0]`, so two near-identical simultaneous inserts bypass it. Either wrap find+update/insert in a transaction (with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to serialize writers) or enforce a UNIQUE index over `tags[0]` for fact kinds and surface the conflict error.

Data-loss bug: two extracted facts can both be judged `update` against the same existing memory, causing the first update to be silently overwritten by the second one. `plan_adjudication` runs independently per fact, so a top-1 candidate can appear for multiple facts; `parse_adjudication` only validates the per-index `existing_id` against the candidate and never checks that the same `existing_id` has already been claimed by an earlier entry. `apply_adjudications` then runs two `find_by_id` + `update_by_id` on the same id in order, clobbering the first fact's content/embedding. Track the set of update targets that have already been claimed in this batch and fall back to `New` on a duplicate (semantic dedup at insert time then either merges or inserts a new row, preserving both facts).

`decay_days` is a public `f64` with no validation. Zero produces `0.0/0.0 = NaN` for same-timestamp items (silently dropped by the `score > 0.0` filter); negative values invert the intended exponential decay and can overflow to `+inf`, letting a single item dominate ranking; `NaN`/`Inf` from upstream config corrupt every score. Either validate (`decay_days.is_finite() && decay_days > 0.0`) in `RankParams::of` or document and treat degenerate values explicitly (e.g. clamp the reciprocal).

`cosine(...).unwrap_or(0.0)` collapses every `None` to a legitimate zero similarity, while the later zero-match guard only checks `query_emb.is_none() || item.embedding.is_none()`. If `cosine` returns `None` for dimension mismatch, zero-norm vector, or non-finite embeddings (instead of "missing"), those items bypass the guard and can still receive positive `importance`/`recency` weights, breaking the documented "zero match → recent fallback" contract. Audit `cosine`'s `None` semantics and either widen the guard to mirror them or propagate the failure as a typed result.
existing_code: let semantic = cosine(query_emb, item.embedding.as_deref()).unwrap_or(0.0);

content: `(now_ms - base) as f64` performs a raw `i64` subtraction on two caller-supplied timestamps. Extreme or corrupted values from persistent storage can overflow: debug builds panic, release builds wrap and the subsequent `max(0.0)` cannot recover the original magnitude, yielding meaningless ages (and `exp` values). Use `checked_sub`/`saturating_sub` and decide on an explicit policy for invalid ages.

The victim DELETE runs in a separate statement before the INSERT, so an INSERT error irreversibly loses the evicted row; also removing only one row per insert never converges when the table already exceeds a lowered capacity (e.g. after tuning capacity is reduced). Wrap the count/victim selection, DELETE, and INSERT in a single transaction and trim down to capacity when needed.

Writers accept embeddings of any dimension, with NaN/Inf components, and zero vectors without validation, even though blob_to_embedding rejects malformed blobs on read. Such vectors are persisted and later returned by load_all, silently breaking semantic dedup (cosine returns None) and retrieval while the insert call reports success. Validate length == EMBED_DIM, finiteness, and non‑zero norm at the shared write boundary.
existing_code:
conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO mem_items (id, kind, content, tags, importance, source, created_at, updated_at, embedding)
         VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3, ?4, ?5, ?6, ?7, ?7, ?8)",
        rusqlite::params![
            id,
            item.kind,
            item.content,
            item.tags.join(","),
            item.importance.clamp(1, 5),
            item.source,
            ts_to_text(now_ms),
            embedding.map(embedding_to_blob),
        ],
    )

content: Cross-key semantic merge overwrites `content` and the full `tags` list, destroying the original key reference (only surfaced via `orig_key`). A semantically-similar write with a different key can silently replace a distinct fact without any source/trust guard. Consider adding a same-key requirement (or stricter source/kind checks) before merge, or at minimum asserting that the target's key can still be looked up after merge.

Near-threshold refusal test only asserts `len == 1` and the outcome variant. It does NOT verify the target row's `content`/`tags` are unchanged. If the implementation performed the merge UPDATE before refusing, the row count stays 1 but the target is silently corrupted and the test would still pass. Add `content` and `tags` assertions on the surviving row.

Mutex poison is swallowed and the lock is salvaged via `e.into_inner()`, then execution continues as if nothing happened. If a previous thread panicked mid-write, the log file can be in an inconsistent state (partial line, missing flush, half-rotated file) yet subsequent audit entries will be appended on top of that corruption. For an audit/security log this is a data-integrity hazard — at minimum, log the poisoning to the audit log itself (or to a fallback sink) before recovering, and consider failing the write so the caller knows the audit line was not durably recorded.

Both filesystem failures are silently dropped: `if let Ok(mut f) = open_log_append(path)` discards the open error, and `let _ = writeln!(f, "[{ts}] {safe}")` discards the write/flush error. For a security/audit trail this is a real data-loss bug — an audit line that fails to open or fails to flush vanishes with no signal to the caller and no fallback record. Surface the error (at least propagate a `Result`, or write a fallback entry to a secondary sink / `eprintln!` with structured context) instead of unconditionally returning `()`.

Per-call working directory is created under `py_runs_root` and never removed. Every successful or failed invocation of `run_dotnet_revisions` permanently leaks a UUID-named directory (plus `params.json`), so disk usage grows unboundedly for any user who triggers the .NET revisions path more than once. Use `tempfile::TempDir` (auto-cleans on drop), or explicitly `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir)` in both the success and error arms before returning, so cleanup happens even when `run_python_at` returns `Err`.

`drain_output` uses stringly-typed dispatch (`if kind == "out"`) and returns a 4-tuple `(String, String, bool, bool)` of anonymous values. A typo or new variant on the producer side silently misroutes stdout into stderr, and the call sites must remember which bool is "got==2" vs "truncated". Replace the `&'static str` channel tag with a shared enum (e.g. `enum Stream { Stdout, Stderr }`) and return a small named struct so the contract is self-evident and type-checked.

`read_capped_drain` swallows the read error: when `read_to_end` fails mid-stream, `buf` is returned with `truncated == false`, so callers cannot distinguish a complete-but-truncated read from an interrupted read that left output incomplete (the comment explicitly warns about "假完整" output). Surface the failure — e.g. return `(Vec<u8>, TruncationStatus)` with a `Complete | Truncated | Interrupted` enum, or return `io::Result<(Vec<u8>, bool)>` — so the caller is forced to handle it instead of silently shipping partial output to the user.

`join_reader_threads` silently detaches the reader thread on timeout: after logging the leak it drops the `JoinHandle` via the `for` loop iteration end, leaving the OS thread running. Because the reader typically owns the `Sender` end of an `mpsc::channel` (and the child's stdout/stderr pipes), a still-running reader will block forever on its next `send` once the receiver is dropped, and the child's pipe FDs / handles stay live in the kernel — producing exactly the kind of "reader_leaked" accumulation this function tries to surface. Either close the receiver-side explicitly before/after the timeout (so the sender errors out and the reader exits), or have the reader thread observe a shared shutdown signal so it actually terminates.

TOCTOU between the symlink check and the subsequent `rename`/`copy_rec`: `symlink_metadata(&src)` is consulted, then later `std::fs::rename(&src, &dest)` (or `copy_rec`) acts on the same path with no atomic guarantee. A concurrent writer can swap a regular file for a symlink inside that window — and the very comment above the check explicitly acknowledges that `rename` would then move the symlink itself into `AI_Gen_Files` while its target stays outside `dir`, defeating the defence. Resolve once and operate on the same handle (e.g. `DirEntry` + `renameat`/`renameat2` with `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, or open with `O_NOFOLLOW` and use `renameat` on the fd) instead of re-stat'ing the path.

`copy_rec` aborts via `?` on the first failing child, but the just-created `dest` directory plus any successfully-copied siblings stay on disk. That contradicts the harvest-rollback path's whole rationale of "no orphan copies". Track whether `create_dir_all(dest)` ran and, on any recursion error, `remove_dir_all(dest)` before propagating the error so callers see a clean all-or-nothing copy.

`sweep_stale_py_runs_in` reports a misleading count: `removed += 1` runs whether or not `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&p)` actually succeeded (the error is discarded by `let _`). Permission errors, locked files on Windows, or transient I/O issues are silently counted as successes and never reach `py_audit`. Increment only on `Ok`, and surface failures — either a second counter for `failed` or per-entry audit lines — so operators can see when stale dirs can't be reaped.

Excel formula-injection guard is incomplete: the comment itself names the threat (WEBSERVICE/DDE on open), but the runtime check only catches cells whose openpyxl data_type is `'f'`. (1) When the model emits values like `'+1+1'`, `'-2+3'`, `'@SUM(...)'` Excel/Calc still evaluate them on open, and openpyxl may persist them as string `'s'` (or worse, as `'f'`) depending on value origin. (2) The guard inspects only the last appended row (`ws[ws.max_row]`); cells added via direct assignment, merges, or later `ws.append` calls later in the iteration are not re-scanned. Recommend sanitizing any string cell value whose first char is in `=+-@` (or its trimmed form starts with one) at write time, and applying the guard to every cell of the appended row (e.g. iterate `ws[ws.max_row]` after each append AND a final sweep over all populated cells).

`file_path_to_string` returns the raw URL for the `Url` variant (e.g. `file:///home/u/a.docx`). That string is then handed to `EXTRACT_SCRIPT` and `MAKE_DOCX_REVISIONS_SCRIPT`, both of which call `os.path.exists(p)` / `docx.Document(p)` / `shutil.copyfile(path, out)`. On POSIX `os.path.exists("file:///...")` is always False, so the script falls through to the "缺少原文" error path even when the user selected a real file via a system dialog that returns the URL form. Convert to a filesystem path (e.g. `url.to_file_path()` / strip the `file://` scheme) before returning, or only return `Some` for the `Path` variant.

Latent bug in `py_gate_acquire_inner`: the second EXITING branch (`*avail += 1`) increments the permit count without a preceding decrement. The comment claims "归还许可" (return permit) but no permit was taken, so if this branch were ever reached under different locking semantics it would leak a phantom permit and let an extra task past the gate. Currently unreachable because both EXITING checks run under the same `PY_PERMITS` mutex guard (the atomic value cannot change between them), but the code does not match its documented intent and is a maintenance hazard.

Output safety / fallback cleanup bug: if `originalPath == outPath`, `File.Copy` throws ("source and destination must not be the same") and the catch then calls `File.Delete(outPath)` — which deletes the user's source document. Separately, when `ReviseInPlace` throws, the partially-edited `outPath` is left in place and `WordprocessingDocument.Create` refuses to overwrite existing files, so the documented "guaranteed fallback" silently fails. Guard against `PathsEqual(originalPath, outPath)` and delete the partial output in the second catch as well.

Leading-insertion position bug: the comment claims a null anchor inserts at the body start, but `body.InsertBefore(para, sect)` puts the paragraph immediately before the section properties — which is the LAST direct child of the body, not the first. `body.Append` likewise appends to the end. New leading content silently lands at the document tail. Insert before the first body child instead.

Non-text run fidelity loss: `UnwrapHyperlinks` permanently removes `w:hyperlink` wrappers so rejecting a revision cannot restore hyperlink targets (only the rPr/Hyperlink style remains). `MarkParagraphDeleted` / `ReviseParagraph` also rebuild runs containing any text using `RunWithText`, which drops `w:sym`, `w:drawing`, `w:footnoteReference`, `w:noBreakHyphen` (mapped to plain `-`), `w:tab`/`w:posTab` distinctions, field-code runs (`w:instrText` / `w:fldChar`), and SDT/customXml content. `InnerRuns` likewise ignores existing `w:ins` / `w:del` wrappers, so the diff is computed against an "accepted" view of the source. Consider preserving hyperlink wrappers around the inserted/deleted runs (they are legal inside `w:ins`/`w:del`) and emitting untouched run children verbatim instead of reconstructing them from `RunText`.

Table-row revisions are not structural: a row "deletion" only wraps the text of each cell paragraph in `w:del` — the row itself is never marked via `<w:trPr><w:del .../>`, so accepting the revision leaves a visibly-empty row in the table. Conversely, row-count changes are emitted by `InsertRevisedParagraph` as ordinary body paragraphs (not new `w:tr` rows with cell paragraphs), and the cell-count mismatch fallback deletes the row and inserts a plain paragraph — destroying the table structure entirely. Use `w:trPr/w:del`/`w:ins` on the row for deletions, and construct real `w:tr` rows (with cells) when the diff asks for a new or replaced row.

Unbounded LCS allocation for paragraph-level diff: `DiffList` always materializes an `(n+1)*(m+1)` `int` matrix with no size cap, unlike `DiffText` which limits itself to 4M cells. With untrusted or large documents (paragraph counts in the tens of thousands), `int[n+1, m+1]` can exceed available memory and crash the process — also a denial-of-service surface if the CLI is fed arbitrary JSON. Apply the same `MaxCells` cap (or fall back to a coarse replace opcode) as `DiffText` does.
